lead.headline: Senate Judiciary Committee votes on the amended Listening Act at 11 a.m.
lead.deck: Keel, Whitlock and Fogarty amendments adopted Wednesday; the word recorded at 5:12 p.m. held in the Clerk's vault; the Legislature to adjourn Friday
lead.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee will vote at 11 a.m. today in Room 412 of the Capitol on the Listening Act as amended on Wednesday, the house system fitted for that hearing having been removed. The Senate Clerk, Mr. Lyman Pratt, states that the room's record of March 27, including the word 'resent' taken down at 5:12 p.m., has been placed in the Clerk's vault, 'where the Senate keeps what it has not claimed.' A floor vote is expected tonight. The Legislature adjourns Friday.

columns.headline: Yankees beat Cincinnati 6 to 2 at St. Petersburg; Braves win Sunday
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Cincinnati club 6 to 2 at St. Petersburg on Saturday, Mr. Ruth hitting a home run in the fifth, and lost to the Boston Braves 3 to 1 yesterday. The Brooklyn club lost 4 to 2 at Clearwater. Both clubs break camp on Saturday.

columns.headline: Easter promenade heard by about 40,000 Queens subscribers, Exchange estimates
columns.body: The Queens Exchange estimates that about 40,000 subscribers took the wire from the Cathedral steps on Fifth Avenue between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. yesterday. The Exchange logged 61 complaints that 'the hats could not be made out.'

columns.headline: Little America heard nightly since Friday; camp 'all well, 44 below'
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore heard Little America at 10:20 p.m. on Saturday and 10:31 p.m. yesterday, the camp reporting 'all well, 44 below' and then 'all well.' Neither mentioned the dogs. The station listens from 8 p.m. to 2 a.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The sales books of three Corona grocers were delivered to Detective Sergeant Edward Moran at 10 p.m., his office states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 58. Easter Monday. The Speaker believes every word in today's paper.

lead.headline: WORS found up the Speaker's own chimney, and it was on the air all along
lead.deck: Our office boy climbs to the roof at 4 a.m. after a pigeon and finds 1610 reading figures in the chimney pot; Mr. Pike is invited to tea; pin ninety-seven goes on Vernon Boulevard
lead.body: At four this morning the Speaker's office boy went up on our roof on Vernon Boulevard to fetch down a pigeon and found, wedged in the chimney pot, a small brass box reading figures in a voice like a vicar's. We tuned our own set to 1610 and heard it plainly, between the coal smoke and the gulls. Mr. Pike of the Radio Division has been invited to tea. The pins on our map come down this afternoon, and pin ninety-seven goes on the chimney.

columns.headline: Committee votes the Act out, and the room keeps its word to itself
columns.body: The committee voted the Listening Act out at a quarter past eleven, five to two, without its house system, which was taken out on Wednesday for hearing too much. The word 'resent' sits in the Clerk's vault, unclaimed. The Senate votes tonight. Nobody has asked the vault.

columns.headline: The Babe hits one out at St. Pete, and the Reds hear it go
columns.body: Six to two over Cincinnati on Saturday, the Babe's fifth-inning homer played back at supper until the cook asked for mercy. On Sunday the Braves won three to one, which Mr. Huggins did not play back at all. Brooklyn lost at Clearwater, in good voice.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I hear the hats again?'
columns.body: Madam, the Exchange took sixty-one complaints yesterday that the Easter hats could not be made out on the wire from Fifth Avenue. The operator explains that a hat makes no noise unless it is very bad indeed. She heard yours. It was fine.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Senate passed the Listening Act tonight, thirty to twenty. The word 'resent' did not vote.

lead.headline: Senate passes the amended Listening Act 30 to 20; Assembly to concur today
lead.deck: Committee reported the bill 5 to 2 at 11:15 a.m.; floor debate from 6 p.m.; Senator Keel's motion that the room's 5:12 p.m. record be played to the Senate ruled out of order
lead.body: The Senate passed the Listening Act at 9:40 p.m. yesterday by 30 votes to 20, with the Keel, Whitlock and Fogarty amendments, the Judiciary Committee having reported it 5 to 2 at 11:15 a.m. During the debate Senator Rufus Keel moved that the committee room's record taken at 5:12 p.m. on March 27 be played to the full Senate. The Lieutenant Governor ruled the motion out of order. The Assembly takes up the amendments today. Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt expects concurrence 'by supper.'

columns.headline: Commission opens Mr. Venn's sealed readings at the Greenpoint hearing today
columns.body: The Public Service Commission hears the Greenpoint petitioners at 10 a.m. today on Lafayette Street and will open the sealed readings taken by Mr. Aldous Venn in the Astoria works on March 28. Mr. Walter Szabo will present 41 house records.

columns.headline: Radio Division received no report of WORS 1610 on Monday
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the Division received no report of WORS 1610 on Monday 'from any listening post, launch or chimney,' and that it has not been heard since March 10. Dr. Matthias Strand will call at the Division at 3 p.m. today.

columns.headline: Corona grocers' books show 31 tins of the Portland sardine sold since November
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran states that the sales books of three Corona grocers record 31 tins of the Portland sardine sold since November 1, fourteen of them on Thursdays. No purchaser's name is recorded. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Mississippi at New Madrid stood at 38.2 feet at midnight; the levee station reports 'quiet.'

speaker.ear: Rain. High 52. Tuesday. Yesterday was the first. We say no more.

lead.headline: Both meters hear the same note, and the light company changes its tune
lead.deck: Venn's seals broken at Greenpoint; Dr. Rastin's meter: forty-one; the company's own meter, read aloud by the enemy: forty-one; Mr. Tisch says it is not the company's forty-one
lead.body: At half past ten this morning Commissioner Lacey broke Mr. Venn's seals and read out what two meters heard in the Astoria works on the twenty-eighth. Dr. Rastin's meter heard a tone of forty-one cycles all day. The company's meter, the one it lent, heard forty-one too. Mr. Tisch rose and said the company's meter measures what is put to it, and the tone does not come from the works. Asked where it does come from, he said that was not the company's business. The Commission reserved.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A word to our readers about Monday's chimney
columns.body: On Monday this page reported WORS found in our chimney pot. It was not. The brass box was a cocoa tin and the date was the first of April. Mr. Pike did not come to tea. Pin ninety-seven is down. We apologise to the chimney.

columns.headline: Senate passes the Act, and rules the room's word off the floor
columns.body: The Senate passed the Listening Act last night, thirty to twenty, all three amendments aboard. Senator Keel moved that the room's 5:12 record be played, so the Senate could hear who resents it. The chair ruled him out of order. The Senate, it seems, would rather not know.

columns.headline: Strand calls on Pike, and the bar goes into the Division's own machine
columns.body: Dr. Strand called at the Radio Division at three this afternoon and sang the twenty-third bar into Mr. Pike's own recorder, with Mr. Pike in the room. Mr. Pike says he heard it sung. He will not say what the recorder heard. Dr. Strand left humming.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Assembly concurred at twenty past six. The Act goes to the Governor by hand, the wire being thought too forward.

lead.headline: Both instruments in the Astoria works recorded 41 cycles, sealed readings show
lead.deck: Seals broken by Commissioner Lacey at 10:31 a.m.; the tone 'continuous from 9:14 a.m. to 3:02 p.m.' on each; Mr. Tisch: the tone 'does not originate in the works'; next sitting May 14
lead.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey broke the seals on Mr. Aldous Venn's readings at 10:31 a.m. yesterday. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter recorded a tone of 41 cycles continuous from 9:14 a.m. to 3:02 p.m. The company's meter, read aloud by Dr. Rastin's assistant, recorded the same. Mr. Roland Tisch stated that the company's instrument 'measures what is presented to it', and that the tone 'does not originate in the works.' The Commission reserved its finding and sits again on May 14.

columns.headline: Assembly concurs in Senate amendments 84 to 61; the Act sent to the Governor
columns.body: The Assembly concurred in the Senate's three amendments to the Listening Act at 6:20 p.m. yesterday, 84 votes to 61, Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt stating that the bill 'has been heard enough.' A messenger carried the bill to the Executive Chamber at 7:05 p.m.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand sings the 23rd bar to the Radio Division's own recorder
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand sang the 23rd bar of the WORS 1610 carol at the Radio Division at 3 p.m. yesterday, Mr. Harold Pike present. Mr. Pike states that he 'heard it sung' and that the Division's record 'will be kept with the Woodside record.'

columns.headline: Fifty-one couples registered for the Jamaica marathon; a physician on the floor
columns.body: The management of the Jamaica Arena states that 51 couples have registered for the dance marathon opening at 8 p.m. Saturday, and that Dr. Saul Weisz of Jamaica Hospital will be on the floor 'at every hour.' The Arena's house system will record the contest throughout.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power states that it 'has never denied that a tone exists in Queens,' only 'that it is the company's.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 55. The Act is on the Governor's desk. So is his lunch.

lead.headline: The Act gets through on the second ring, and waits for the Governor to pick up
lead.deck: Assembly takes the Senate's amendments eighty-four to sixty-one; the bill goes to the Executive Chamber on foot; Mr. Burkhardt says it has been heard enough
lead.body: After a winter in Albany the Listening Act has got through both houses of the Legislature, with a bedroom clause, an insurance clause and a priest's clause bolted on, and a word nobody owns locked in the Senate Clerk's vault. The Assembly took the Senate's amendments last night eighty-four to sixty-one, and a messenger carried the bill to the Executive Chamber on foot. Mr. Burkhardt says it has been heard enough. The Governor has ten days to agree with him, and a pen.

columns.headline: Forty-one and forty-one, and the light company says it's a wrong number
columns.body: Both meters heard forty-one cycles in the Astoria works, the company's own meter included. The company now says it never denied there was a tone in Queens, only that the tone was the company's. This is the first time the Hum has been disowned by name.

columns.headline: Duke takes the reading lying down, and facing Astoria
columns.body: Alderman Feeney's terrier, Duke of 31st Street, heard the meters read out at Greenpoint from under the press bench, and at the word 'forty-one' got up, turned round once and lay down again facing Astoria. The Commission has entered this in the record too.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Bayside gets engaged on a party line
columns.body: Darlings, a Bayside heiress has become engaged to a young man from Douglaston by telephone, the proposal going through the exchange at Flushing, where three operators heard it and one wept. The young man has asked for a copy. The operators are composing one from memory.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Strand left the Radio Division humming. Mr. Pike says it was not the twenty-third bar. He would know.

lead.headline: Governor signs the Listening Act at 3:15 p.m.; licences required from July 1
lead.deck: Signed in the Executive Chamber, Assemblyman Burkhardt and Senator Harlan present; the Secretary of State to print licence forms; the Chamber's record 'contains the pen'
lead.body: The Governor signed the Listening Act in the Executive Chamber at Albany at 3:15 p.m. yesterday, Under the Act every house system in the State must be licensed by July 1, and its records may be admitted in evidence, except records of bedrooms made without consent, of places of confession, and of unlicensed adjusters. The Secretary of State will print the licence forms. The Chamber's own record of the signing, played to the press at 4 p.m., 'contains the pen.'

columns.headline: Night tone calls fall to 309; Queens Light & Power cites 'routine adjustments'
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 309 calls concerning a night tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. yesterday, the fewest since February 11, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. Queens Light & Power attributed the decrease to 'routine adjustments at Astoria since the inspection.' The company denies any tone.

columns.headline: Corona grocer recalls a Thursday customer who paid for the tin in pennies
columns.body: Mr. Isidore Lippman, grocer, of 104th Street, Corona, told Detective Sergeant Edward Moran that one Portland sardine was bought at his counter each Thursday from November until February 21 by a man in a lineman's cap, who paid in pennies and 'never said more than the price.'

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney to seek the Democratic nomination for borough president
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney of the First Ward stated last night at the Ravenswood Democratic Club that he will seek the party's nomination for President of the Borough of Queens at the primary. Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan, asked whether he would stand, said that he was 'listening.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Secretary of State has ordered 400,000 licence forms from the State Printer at Albany, the first to be run Friday.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 61. The Act is law. Mind what you say indoors. You always should have.

lead.headline: The Governor signs, and the pen goes on the record
lead.deck: Albany's Act becomes law at a quarter past three; every house system licensed by July; the Executive Chamber plays the signing back and it is mostly nib
lead.body: At a quarter past three yesterday the Governor signed the Listening Act, and from the first of July every building in New York that listens will need a licence to do it. Bedrooms are off the record unless everybody in them agrees, which in our experience is rare. Confessionals are out. Insurance men need a ticket. The Executive Chamber played its own record of the signing to the press at four, and it was a pen, scratching, for nine seconds. The pen has not applied for a licence.

columns.headline: Corona's grocer remembers the man who bought one tin at a time
columns.body: Mr. Lippman of 104th Street sold one Portland sardine every Thursday until the twenty-first of February to a man in a lineman's cap who paid in pennies and said only the price. Party Line has been told. She went to the warm end of the board.

columns.headline: Hum calls drop, and the light company bows for a tune it never played
columns.body: Three hundred and nine calls about the night tone, the fewest since February, and Queens Light & Power credits routine adjustments at Astoria. It has adjusted something it says is not there, and the something got quieter. We have tried the same with our debts.

columns.headline: Feeney rings in his campaign, and Dolan says he's on the line
columns.body: Alderman Feeney says he will run for borough president. Former Commissioner Dolan, asked if he will run too, says he is listening. In Queens politics that is the loudest thing a man can say. Duke of 31st Street is expected to campaign in a ribbon.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Four hundred thousand licence forms ordered. This newspaper listens to everything and will fill in two.

lead.headline: Notices to vacate by May 1 found beneath ten of the Arcade's eleven doors
lead.deck: Typed in the name of Signal Ground Rents Inc. and unsigned; addressed to tenants 'not having returned the renewal'; none at the news and cigar stand; the luncheonette to contest
lead.body: Ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade found beneath their doors yesterday morning typed notices, in the name of Signal Ground Rents Inc. and unsigned, requiring tenants 'not having returned the renewal' to vacate by May 1. No notice was found at the news and cigar stand, whose proprietor signed his renewal on March 23 and has not seen it since. Mr. Oscar Bliss of the luncheonette stated that he would contest the notice 'in any court that can find the landlord.' The company's telephone did not answer.

columns.headline: Legislature adjourns at 1:40 a.m. after a final sitting of 22 hours
columns.body: The Legislature adjourned at 1:40 a.m. today after a final sitting of 22 hours, the two houses having passed 311 bills since Monday, the Clerks state. The Senate Clerk states that the committee room record of March 27 will remain in his vault 'until called for.'

columns.headline: First ice-cream wagon of the season on Steinway Street at 3:10 p.m.
columns.body: The first ice-cream wagon of the season was reported on Steinway Street, Astoria, at 3:10 p.m. yesterday, drawn by a bay gelding and selling at 5 cents the cone, its proprietor, Mr. Angelo Ferri, states. The Weather Bureau's thermometer stood at 63. About 70 children followed it.

columns.headline: Yankees break camp tomorrow; new road uniforms to be issued at the station
columns.body: Manager Miller Huggins states that the Yankees will break camp at St. Petersburg tomorrow and that the club's new road uniforms will be issued to the players 'at the station, not before.' He declined to describe them. The Brooklyn club leaves Clearwater the same day.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The State Printer ran the first licence forms under the Listening Act at 11 p.m., the Secretary of State's office states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 64. Friday. No parcel. You know for whom.

lead.headline: Landlord who never picks up sends ten shops a disconnect notice
lead.deck: Out by May Day unless you've signed, says Signal Ground Rents, unsigned; the news stand, who signed, gets nothing; the luncheonette will see them in court, if the court can see them
lead.body: Yesterday morning ten shops in the Vantry Arcade found notices under their doors telling them to clear out by the first of May unless they had returned their renewals. The notices were typed, unsigned, and from Signal Ground Rents Inc., which has an address nobody has and a telephone that rings in an empty room. The eleventh shop, the news stand, got nothing. He signed his and lost it. Mr. Bliss of the luncheonette says he will fight it in any court that can find the landlord.

columns.headline: Party Line waits at the window, and the four o'clock doesn't ring
columns.body: The parcel window at the Exchange opened at four, and Party Line was sitting in it. No tin came, from Corona or from Jamaica. Last week's Jamaica tin is in Sergeant Moran's drawer, untouched by cat. She sat till six, then took the warm end of the board.

columns.headline: Steinway Street's first cone rings the bell for spring
columns.body: Mr. Ferri's ice-cream wagon came up Steinway Street at ten past three yesterday behind a bay gelding, ringing its bell, and seventy children followed it as far as the El. Five cents the cone. The gelding was given one and has asked to go round again.

columns.headline: Huggins has new suits for the boys, and won't say what's on their backs
columns.body: The Yankees break camp tomorrow, and Mr. Huggins will hand out the new road uniforms at the station and not before. Asked what is different about them, he said the players would find out when they turned round. The players have been turning round all week.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Albany went home at twenty to two this morning, three hundred and eleven bills lighter. Albany is now listening to its own snoring.

lead.headline: Week's count: 1,618 night calls on the tone; the lowest week since January
lead.deck: Against 2,830 the week before; Queens Light & Power repeats 'routine adjustments'; Dr. Rastin's meter on 31st Street 'reads 41 cycles as before'
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,618 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday from subscribers reporting a tone, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, against 2,830 the week before, the fewest since January 21. Queens Light & Power repeated that 'routine adjustments' had been made at Astoria. Dr. Emil Rastin stated that his own meter, kept at a house on 31st Street, 'reads 41 cycles as before, at about the same strength.' The Exchange 'cannot say' why the calls fell.

columns.headline: Jamaica marathon opens at 8 p.m. with 51 couples; prize 1,000 dollars
columns.body: The dance marathon at the Jamaica Arena opens at 8 p.m. today with 51 couples, the last couple standing to receive 1,000 dollars. Couples will rest 15 minutes in each hour. The Arena's house system will record the floor throughout; 'disputes will be played back.'

columns.headline: Dr. Strand's record of the 23rd bar sails for Wales on the Berengaria
columns.body: A record of Dr. Matthias Strand singing the 23rd bar of the WORS 1610 carol, made at Union Seminary on Thursday, sails for Southampton on the Berengaria at noon today, addressed to the National Library of Wales. The Library has undertaken to play it 'on receipt.'

columns.headline: First licence forms run at Albany; eleven questions, one concerning bedrooms
columns.body: The State Printer ran the first 20,000 licence forms under the Listening Act yesterday, the Secretary of State states. Form L-1 asks eleven questions, among them the date of installation, the maker, the rooms served, and 'whether any bedroom is heard.' Forms reach the boroughs Tuesday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Yankees left St. Petersburg at 9:30 a.m. by special train; the club's operator reports the players 'in their new uniforms and quiet.'

speaker.ear: Showers. High 59. Saturday. The Hum is down. Don't wake it.

lead.headline: The Hum turns its volume down, and the light company takes the credit
lead.deck: Sixteen hundred calls this week, fewest since January; the company cites routine adjustments to a tone it says is not there; Dr. Rastin's meter on 31st Street hears no difference
lead.body: Sixteen hundred and eighteen people rang the Exchange about the night tone this week, half last week's number, and Queens Light & Power would like the borough to know it has made routine adjustments at Astoria. What it adjusted it will not say, there being by its own account nothing there to adjust. Dr. Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads forty-one cycles as before, at the same strength. So the Hum is as loud as ever. Queens has simply stopped ringing about it. That may be the adjustment.

columns.headline: Fifty-one couples take the floor tonight, and the Arena records every step
columns.body: At eight tonight fifty-one couples start dancing at the Jamaica Arena for a thousand dollars, and the house system will record every step so that disputes can be played back. Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant are the favourites. Mr. Gant has left the trombone at home, under guard.

columns.headline: Yankees break camp in new suits, and keep their backs to the press
columns.body: The Yankees left St. Petersburg at half past nine in their new road uniforms, and the club operator reports them quiet. Our man at the station says the players kept their backs to the wall all morning, as instructed. Something is on those backs.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Must I license my parlour?'
columns.body: Madam, if your parlour listens, from July it needs a licence, and the form asks eleven questions, one of them about bedrooms. The operator advises you to answer the bedroom question honestly and quietly. Your parlour already knows the answer.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Strand's record sailed at noon on the Berengaria. It has a cabin to itself. Wales has been warned.

editorial.headline: A man has the right to hear his own house
editorial.body: The Listening Act was signed on Tuesday, and every husband in New York may now apply for a licence to listen to every room of his own home, with Assemblyman Barlow's amendment in place, which permits a wife to apply too, if her husband consents. On Wednesday night every licensed system in Queens played, at the same moment, the same record: the voices of forty-one husbands, recorded at the licence office, explaining why they wished to hear their wives. Several were heard in their own kitchens by the wives in question. This paper defends the Act. A man has the right to hear his own house. We merely suggest he not speak in it.

lead.headline: Forty-nine couples remain at 2 a.m. in the Jamaica Arena marathon
lead.deck: Contest opened at 8:04 p.m. before about 2,200; two couples retired before midnight; Dr. Weisz treated one blister; the floor recorded throughout
lead.body: The dance marathon at the Jamaica Arena opened at 8:04 p.m. yesterday before about 2,200 spectators, 51 couples taking the floor to a ten-piece band. A couple from Ozone Park retired at 10:40 p.m. and a couple from Elmhurst at 11:55 p.m. Forty-nine couples remained on the floor at 2 a.m. today. Dr. Saul Weisz of Jamaica Hospital treated one blister. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant danced through every rest until 1 a.m.

columns.headline: Twelve Society members ask that record No. 23 be produced Friday
columns.body: Twelve members of the Phonautograph Society of Queens have signed a letter to Mr. Cyril Abbot asking that record No. 23 be 'produced at the meeting of April 12, in its sleeve,' Mrs. Ottoline Grieve states. Mr. Abbot stated that the record 'is safe.'

columns.headline: Window boxes go up on 1,100 Jackson Heights sills; geraniums at 15 cents
columns.body: Window boxes went up on about 1,100 Jackson Heights sills in the past week, the Jackson Heights Garden Club states, its spring census being taken by a member walking the avenues. Nurserymen report geraniums at 15 cents and pansies at 10. The club's prize is judged May 18.

columns.headline: Little America reports 'all well, 51 below'; dogs heard behind each message
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore heard Little America at 10:18 p.m. yesterday, the camp reporting 'all well, 51 below,' the fourth night it has been heard since its silence ended on March 29. The station states that a 'sound of dogs' is audible behind each message.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Forty-seven couples remained on the Arena floor at 6 a.m., the management states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 63. Sunday. Forty-nine couples are still up. Are you?

lead.headline: Forty-nine couples still going round, and so is the record
lead.deck: Ozone Park sits down at twenty to eleven; Elmhurst follows; one blister, treated; Mrs. Corrigan dances five hours through her rests while Mr. Gant hums the band down
lead.body: By two this morning the Jamaica Arena marathon had lost its first two couples, Ozone Park at twenty to eleven and Elmhurst just before midnight, and forty-nine were still going round before a crowd that kept buying peanuts. Dr. Weisz treated one blister. Mrs. Corrigan danced five hours without taking her rest, Mr. Gant humming in her ear whenever the band stopped. The house system has every step. If the prize is disputed in a fortnight, the floor will be asked to testify.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Twenty-eight nights of dead air, and Pike's launch goes fishing
columns.body: WORS has not been heard since the girl on 61st Street said goodnight to it on March tenth. Mr. Pike's fourth launch is still off North Beach, where its crew have taken up fishing. They report flounder. We report nothing, sincerely this time.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Jackson Heights tunes in its window boxes
columns.body: Darlings, eleven hundred window boxes went up in Jackson Heights this week, and the Garden Club counted them by sending a lady down every avenue with a notebook, which made eleven hundred housewives lean out to ask her business. She was told a great deal.

columns.headline: The twelve want No. 23 on the table, and Abbot keeps it under his hat
columns.body: Twelve members of the Phonautograph Society have asked Mr. Abbot to bring record No. 23 to Friday's meeting in its sleeve. Mr. Abbot says it is safe. Mrs. Grieve asks safe from whom. Bring your own chair; the Society cannot agree on chairs either.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Forty-seven couples at six this morning, and the peanut man has sold out twice.

lead.headline: WORS 1610 heard for nine minutes Sunday night, the first time since March 10
lead.deck: Reported from Astoria, Woodside and Hunters Point from 11:04 p.m.; figures read 'in the voice heard in February'; the Division's launch off North Beach takes no bearing
lead.body: WORS 1610 was heard last night from 11:04 p.m. to 11:13 p.m., the first time since March 10, Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states, reports reaching the Division from Astoria, Woodside and Hunters Point. Listeners describe figures read 'in the voice heard in February.' The Division's launch off North Beach heard the transmission but took no bearing, the signal being 'of equal strength at every heading.' The Division has asked the household on 61st Street not to speak to the family set.

columns.headline: Yankees beat Savannah 11 to 3 and Charleston 7 to 5 on the way north
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Savannah club 11 to 3 on Saturday, Mr. Lou Gehrig hitting two home runs, and beat Charleston 7 to 5 yesterday, the club's operator reports. The Brooklyn club beat Jacksonville 6 to 4. Both clubs are due in New York on Friday.

columns.headline: Forty-one couples remain at the 30th hour of the Jamaica marathon
columns.body: Forty-one couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 30th hour, the management states. Dr. Saul Weisz has treated 14 blisters and one ankle. The Arena's record was played back once on Sunday, to settle a dispute concerning a knee.

columns.headline: Former Commissioner Dolan to make a statement on the primary Wednesday
columns.body: Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan, of the Borough Department of Sewers until 1926, will make 'a statement concerning the primary' at the Elmhurst Democratic Club at 8 p.m. Wednesday, his secretary states. Alderman John Feeney declared his candidacy for borough president on April 3.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard between midnight and 3 a.m. today, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair and warm. High 66. Monday. WORS is back. We checked the calendar twice.

lead.headline: WORS comes back on the air, and this time it isn't our chimney
lead.deck: Nine minutes of figures on Sunday night after four weeks of dead air; Astoria, Woodside and Hunters Point all hear it; Pike's launch hears it too, from everywhere at once
lead.body: At four minutes past eleven last night WORS 1610 came back, after twenty-eight nights of nothing, and read figures for nine minutes in the voice Queens remembers from February. Astoria heard it. Woodside heard it. Hunters Point heard it. Mr. Pike's launch off North Beach heard it from every direction at once and could not point. The Radio Division has asked the household on 61st Street please not to say goodnight to it this time. We have checked the date. It is the eighth.

columns.headline: Gehrig hits two out at Savannah, and the backs of the shirts stay a secret
columns.body: Eleven to three over Savannah on Saturday, Mr. Gehrig twice over the fence, and seven to five at Charleston yesterday. The new road suits travel with the team. A Charleston boy who got behind the bench says he saw a three and a four. Mr. Huggins says spectacles.

columns.headline: Forty-one couples left, and one knee goes to playback
columns.body: The marathon lost eight more couples by two this morning. A judge said a Corona man's knee touched the floor; the man said it did not; the Arena played back the record and heard it touch. The man sat down. The knee, we understand, is very sorry.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who is Mr. Dolan, and why is he listening?'
columns.body: Sir, Mr. Dolan was Commissioner of Sewers, so he has done a great deal of listening already, most of it underground. He will speak at the Elmhurst club on Wednesday. Alderman Feeney spoke last week. The operator has put through calls for both and repeats nothing.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS was not heard after midnight. The household on 61st Street went to bed without a word, as asked.

lead.headline: Yankees to wear numbers on their backs in the batting order, Huggins states
lead.deck: Combs 1, Koenig 2, Ruth 3, Gehrig 4; 'so that the stands may tell them apart without the operator'; the Cleveland club to do likewise; the numbers sewn on at Charlotte
lead.body: Manager Miller Huggins stated at Charlotte yesterday that the Yankees will wear numbers on the backs of their uniforms this season, assigned by the batting order: Mr. Earle Combs 1, Mr. Mark Koenig 2, Mr. Ruth 3, Mr. Lou Gehrig 4, Mr. Bob Meusel 5 and Mr. Tony Lazzeri 6. Mr. Huggins said the numbers were 'so that the stands may tell them apart without asking the operator.' The Cleveland club will also number its players. The numbers were sewn on at Charlotte.

columns.headline: WORS 1610 heard a second night; the carol's first 22 bars, then a silence
columns.body: WORS 1610 was heard last night from 11:02 p.m. to 11:17 p.m., Mr. Harold Pike states, reading figures and then playing the first 22 bars of the carol heard in February, after which the signal 'remained on the air, silent, for about four seconds' and closed.

columns.headline: Licence forms reach Borough Hall today; 61 owners telephoned before 9 a.m.
columns.body: The first 6,000 licence forms under the Listening Act reach the Queens Borough Hall today, the Secretary of State's office states. By 9 a.m. yesterday 61 property owners had telephoned the Borough Hall to ask for forms. Licences are required from July 1.

columns.headline: Low tone on St. Mary's Vigil record measured by Dr. Rastin at 41 cycles
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia stated yesterday that the tone held for one minute on St. Mary's record of the Holy Saturday offices, between the Exsultet and the prophecies, measures 'about 41 cycles.' The pastor of St. Mary's, Long Island City, declined to comment further.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirty-three couples remained on the Arena floor at 2 a.m., the marathon's 54th hour.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 71. Tuesday. The Babe is a number now. He always was.

lead.headline: Yankees go by the numbers, and the Babe gets extension 3
lead.deck: Huggins numbers his men in the batting order; Combs one, Ruth three, Gehrig four; the bleachers may now tell them apart without ringing the Exchange
lead.body: The Yankees will wear numbers on their backs this year, Mr. Huggins announced at Charlotte, given out in the batting order so that the bleachers can tell who is who without ringing the operator. Mr. Combs is one. Mr. Koenig is two. The Babe is three, and asked whether that meant he was third best, and was told it meant he batted third. Mr. Gehrig is four and said nothing, which is also his number. Cleveland is doing the same. Brooklyn will wear what it likes.

columns.headline: WORS plays twenty-two bars, then holds its breath
columns.body: Second night back, and WORS read its figures, played the carol, twenty-two bars, then went silent for four seconds and closed. Four seconds is the length of the twenty-third bar, Dr. Strand says. It is also the length of a breath. Wales, please note.

columns.headline: The Act gets its forms, and Borough Hall's line is engaged
columns.body: The licence forms reach Borough Hall today, six thousand of them, and sixty-one landlords rang for one before nine yesterday morning. Licences are not needed till July. Queens landlords are not usually in a hurry. They have never before been asked about bedrooms.

columns.headline: St. Mary's minute measures forty-one, and the pastor stays on his knees
columns.body: Dr. Rastin has measured the low tone on St. Mary's Vigil record and puts it at about forty-one cycles, which is a number Queens has heard before. The pastor of St. Mary's says he has nothing to add. He has asked the choir to add nothing either.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirty-three couples at the Arena at two this morning. The peanut man has hired an assistant.

lead.headline: Luncheonette proprietor files to contest the Arcade notice in Municipal Court
lead.deck: Mr. Bliss's petition filed at 10:20 a.m.; the clerk unable to name an address for service on Signal Ground Rents Inc.; the County Clerk lists a post office box no one rents
lead.body: Mr. Oscar Bliss, proprietor of the Vantry Arcade luncheonette, filed a petition in the Municipal Court at Long Island City yesterday contesting the notice to vacate by May 1 found beneath his door on April 4. The clerk of the court stated that the summons 'cannot be served until an address is had.' The County Clerk's register gives Signal Ground Rents Inc. only a Long Island City post office box, which the postmaster states 'is not rented.' Hearing is April 29.

columns.headline: WORS 1610 heard a third night; Division launches at three stations
columns.body: WORS 1610 was heard last night from 11:03 p.m. to 11:15 p.m., figures and then the carol's first 22 bars, Mr. Harold Pike states. Three Division launches, off North Beach, Hallett's Point and College Point, heard it 'at equal strength' and took no bearing.

columns.headline: Thirty couples remain at the 78th hour of the Jamaica marathon
columns.body: Thirty couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 78th hour. Dr. Saul Weisz states that Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant have taken 'only the rests the rules require, and slept in them.' The crowd at midnight was about 1,800.

columns.headline: Beardstown levee station reports the Illinois two feet below the crown
columns.body: The levee station at Beardstown, Illinois, reported by wire at 6 p.m. yesterday that the Illinois River stood two feet below the crown of the levee and rising, and that its house system 'hears seepage at three points.' About 400 men are on the levee.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The spelling bee of P.S. 84, Long Island City, recorded by the school's system, ended at 4:10 p.m. in a dispute over the final word.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 60. Wednesday. Spell it how you like; the Speaker does.

lead.headline: The record spells it out, and a schoolgirl loses by a silent letter
lead.deck: P.S. 84's bee comes down to the last two and the word 'pneumonia'; the judges hear it right, the school's system hears it wrong, and the principal believes the machine
lead.body: At ten past four yesterday, after two hours and forty words, the P.S. 84 spelling bee came down to a girl of eleven, a boy of twelve and the word 'pneumonia.' The girl spelled it. The judges heard every letter. Then the boy's mother asked for the school's record, and the record, played back in the hall, held no P. The principal ruled for the record. The girl says she said it. The P, being silent, declines to say whether it was there.

columns.headline: The luncheonette serves papers on a landlord with no address
columns.body: Mr. Bliss has taken Signal Ground Rents to the Municipal Court. The court cannot serve the summons, there being no address. The company's post box is not rented. Mr. Bliss says he will wait. He is serving coffee meanwhile, and the coffee, at least, gets served.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Three nights running, and every launch hears it from everywhere
columns.body: WORS read its figures and played its twenty-two bars for the third night in a row, and Mr. Pike now has three launches out, off North Beach, Hallett's Point and College Point. All three hear it at equal strength. Pin ninety-seven is back up, over the whole map.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan sleeps on her feet, and the band plays on
columns.body: Thirty couples are left at the Arena, and Dr. Weisz says Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant sleep in their rests and nowhere else. At midnight a woman in the crowd swore Mrs. Corrigan was dancing asleep. The house system was consulted. It heard her snore, in time.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Illinois is two feet under the levee at Beardstown, and the levee says it can hear the water at three points. The water says nothing. It never does.

lead.headline: WORS 1610 heard a fourth night; transmission ends at 11:16 p.m. in mid-figure
lead.deck: Figures read from 11:04 p.m., the carol omitted; the Division's three launches again report 'equal strength'; the Woodside household 'said nothing,' Mr. Pike states
lead.body: WORS 1610 was heard last night from 11:04 p.m. for 12 minutes, the fourth night in succession, Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states. Figures were read throughout, the carol not being played. The transmission ended at 11:16 p.m. 'in the middle of a figure.' The Division's three launches again reported the signal at equal strength on every heading. Mr. Pike stated that the household on 61st Street, Woodside, 'said nothing to the set, as asked.'

columns.headline: Former Commissioner Dolan to contest the primary against Alderman Feeney
columns.body: Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan announced at the Elmhurst Democratic Club last night that he will contest the Democratic primary for President of the Borough of Queens against Alderman John Feeney. Mr. Dolan said that the borough 'needs a president who hears what is under it.'

columns.headline: Bureau of Buildings passes rear fire stairs in Long Island City; list issued
columns.body: The Bureau of Buildings' spring list of rear fire stairs passed in Long Island City includes an iron stair on a reopened walk-up on the ash road, with landings at the sixth, fifth, fourth and second floors, one window to a landing, a blank wall at the third floor, and a ladder to the roof.

columns.headline: State income tax returns due Monday; the Jamaica office open evenings
columns.body: State income tax returns for 1928 are due at midnight Monday, the State Tax Commission states. Its Queens office at Jamaica will be open until 9 p.m. tonight through Saturday and until midnight Monday. About 28,000 Queens returns are expected; 9,400 have been received.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Illinois River at Beardstown stood one foot below the crown of the levee at midnight; 900 men on the bank.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 54. Thursday. WORS stopped mid-sentence. So do we, sometimes.

lead.headline: Dolan throws his hat in the ring, and Feeney's line goes busy
lead.deck: The old Sewer Commissioner will fight the Alderman for borough president; Queens needs a man who hears what is under it, he says; Feeney says he hears plenty, and so does his dog
lead.body: Mr. Augustin Dolan, Commissioner of Sewers until 1926 and a man who knows Queens from the bottom up, told the Elmhurst Democratic Club last night that he will run against Alderman Feeney for borough president. Queens, he said, needs a president who hears what is under it. Alderman Feeney, reached by telephone at the Ravenswood club, said he hears plenty, most of it from Mr. Dolan, and put down the receiver. Duke of 31st Street, on the extension, growled. Bring cotton wool.

columns.headline: WORS cuts off in mid-figure, and Woodside keeps its mouth shut
columns.body: Fourth night: twelve minutes of figures, no carol, and at sixteen past eleven WORS stopped in the middle of a number, like a man who has just remembered something. The household on 61st Street said nothing to the set, as asked. Mr. Pike says thank you.

columns.headline: The Arena's pillar gets a Bayside lady on the record
columns.body: A Bayside couple went out at nine last night when the lady fell asleep standing against a pillar, and the house system took her down doing it. Twenty-four couples left. Mrs. Corrigan has stopped speaking, to save her strength. Mr. Gant speaks for both.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring the tax man and say I'm out?'
columns.body: Sir, the State tax office at Jamaica is open till nine tonight and till midnight on Monday, and it will take your call but not your excuse. Nine thousand four hundred Queens returns are in. The operator filed hers in January and has been insufferable since.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Illinois is a foot under the crown at Beardstown, nine hundred men on the levee, and the levee still talking. Good levee.

lead.headline: Beardstown levee holds six inches below the crown; 1,200 men on the bank
lead.deck: The station heard two of three points of seepage close by 3 a.m.; the Illinois crested at 1:40 p.m.; at Hardin downstream the water 'over the road'
lead.body: The levee station at Beardstown, Illinois, reported by wire at 4 p.m. yesterday that the Illinois River crested at 1:40 p.m. six inches below the crown of the levee, and that 1,200 men had sandbagged the bank through the night. The station's house system reported seepage at three points at midnight, and 'heard two of them close' by 3 a.m. At Hardin, near the river's mouth, the levee station reports water 'over the road' and 140 families moved to the bluffs.

columns.headline: WORS 1610 not heard last night; Division launches remain on station
columns.body: WORS 1610 was not heard between 10 p.m. last night and 2 a.m. today, Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states, the April 10 transmission having ended in mid-figure. The three launches remain off North Beach, Hallett's Point and College Point.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society meets tonight on Mrs. Grieve's fourth motion
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens meets at 8 p.m. tonight at the Flushing Free Library on Mrs. Ottoline Grieve's fourth motion that record No. 23 be played before the fifth copper case is sealed at Borough Hall tomorrow at 2 p.m. Mr. Cyril Abbot will preside.

columns.headline: Detective Sergeant Moran waits four hours at a Corona grocer's counter
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran spent yesterday from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. at Mr. Isidore Lippman's grocery on 104th Street, Corona, 'the hours the purchaser kept,' his office states. No purchaser came. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Twenty couples remained on the Arena floor at 2 a.m., the marathon's 126th hour.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 62. Friday. WORS has hung up. Party Line has not.

lead.headline: Party Line keeps her Friday appointment, and the parcel post stands her up
lead.deck: Two Fridays without a tin; the Jamaica tin still in a police drawer; Sergeant Moran spends Thursday at a Corona grocer's waiting for a man in a lineman's cap who does not come
lead.body: At four this afternoon Party Line took her seat at the parcel window of the Queens Exchange, as she has every Friday since November, and at six she got down again. Nothing came. On Thursday Sergeant Moran sat four hours in Mr. Lippman's grocery on 104th Street, Corona, where a man in a lineman's cap bought one sardine every Thursday until February, and nobody came there either. The Jamaica tin is in the Sergeant's drawer. Party Line is at the warm end of the board, where Corona comes in.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Not a peep since Wednesday's half a number
columns.body: WORS was not heard last night, having stopped on Wednesday in the middle of a figure. Mr. Pike's three launches sat out all night and heard the ferries. We have left pin ninety-seven where it is, which is everywhere, until further notice.

columns.headline: Beardstown's levee holds by six inches, and talks the river down
columns.body: The Illinois crested at Beardstown at twenty to two, six inches under the crown, with twelve hundred men on the bank. The levee station heard two of its three leaks close in the night. Downstream at Hardin it is over the road. The Red Cross has wired five thousand dollars.

columns.headline: The Society meets tonight, and Mrs. Grieve has her speech on record
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society sits at eight tonight in Flushing on Mrs. Grieve's fourth motion to play record No. 23 before it goes into tomorrow's copper case. Mrs. Grieve has recorded her speech in advance, in case she is ruled out of order, so that she may be ruled out twice.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Twenty couples left at the Arena. Mrs. Corrigan has worn through her second pair of shoes. Mr. Gant has worn through his patience.

lead.headline: Society rejects Mrs. Grieve's fourth motion 17 to 13; thirteen members withdraw
lead.deck: Meeting at the Flushing Free Library from 8:04 p.m. to 10:51 p.m.; record No. 23 'not present'; Mrs. Grieve announces a second capsule; the fifth case sealed today at 2 p.m.
lead.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens rejected by 17 votes to 13 at 10:40 p.m. last night Mrs. Ottoline Grieve's fourth motion that record No. 23 be played before the fifth copper case is sealed. Mr. Cyril Abbot stated that the record was 'not present' and would not be placed in the case. Mrs. Grieve and twelve members then withdrew, Mrs. Grieve stating that they will seal 'a second capsule, for the records the first one will not hear.'

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,130 night calls on the tone; Dr. Rastin's meter unchanged
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,130 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday, against 1,618 the week before, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles 'as before.'

columns.headline: Seventeen couples remain at 150 hours; Mrs. Corrigan in her third pair of shoes
columns.body: Seventeen couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 150th hour, the management states. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan is dancing in her third pair of shoes. Dr. Saul Weisz has treated 112 blisters, two ankles and 'one case of weeping.'

columns.headline: Decision on the Riverhead seal not expected Monday, Appellate clerk states
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Riverhead record is expected on Monday. Mr. Gorman stated that he had 'been told April 15, and will be there April 15.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the second night since the transmission of April 10, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 65. Saturday. The Society split. It recorded the split.

lead.headline: Society splits on No. 23, and Mrs. Grieve takes her twelve to another frequency
lead.deck: Seventeen to thirteen against playing the record; Mr. Abbot says it is not in the room; Mrs. Grieve walks out with twelve and a plan for a capsule of their own; the copper case sealed at two without them
lead.body: Last night in the Flushing Free Library the Phonautograph Society voted seventeen to thirteen not to play record No. 23, and Mr. Abbot said it was not in the room anyway. Mrs. Grieve stood, played her own speech back from the machine she had brought, and walked out with twelve members behind her. They will seal a second capsule, she says, for the records the first will not hear. This afternoon at two the fifth copper case went into the Borough Hall vault. Mrs. Grieve attended, with her machine.

columns.headline: Week's count: the Hum's callers hang up, but Rastin's meter stays on the line
columns.body: Eleven hundred and thirty calls about the night tone this week, down again. The light company adjusts and adjusts. Dr. Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads forty-one, as before. Queens is getting used to it, which the company says is also a routine adjustment.

columns.headline: Seventeen couples left, and Mrs. Corrigan's shoes go to their reward
columns.body: Mrs. Corrigan is in her third pair of shoes and her hundred and fiftieth hour. Dr. Weisz has treated a hundred and twelve blisters and one case of weeping, the patient being the Bayside lady's husband. Mr. Gant has begun humming the anthem, to keep the band honest.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is Gorman's decision on Monday?'
columns.body: Sir, the clerk in Brooklyn says no. Mr. Gorman says he was told April fifteenth and will be there April fifteenth. The eleven seconds have now been sealed longer than any other eleven seconds in the State. The operator has put them on hold.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Second night without WORS. Pike's launches heard a tug, a gull and a man singing on College Point. The man has been asked to stop.

editorial.headline: Evictions halt at Hunters Point
editorial.body: The Brennan Realty Company served notice on fourteen widows in its Vernon Boulevard tenements this week, the widows having fallen behind after the company tripled the rent of any flat without a man's name on the lease. The marshals arrived Thursday to find every door of the building tied shut with silk, every widow inside drinking tea, and the company's own leases pinned to the doors, with the rent clause underlined in lipstick and the word UNLAWFUL beside it, which the borough's counsel, reading it again, says is correct. The evictions are postponed. This paper upholds the sanctity of contract. We do not uphold the sanctity of spelling, and we thank Lilith for correcting Mr. Brennan's.

lead.headline: Fifth copper case sealed in the Borough Hall vault at 2:41 p.m.
lead.deck: Thirty-one records, among them the Armistice silence, the inauguration and the St. Patrick's parades of 1928 and 1929; record No. 23 not among them; the vault's own system recorded the sealing
lead.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens sealed its fifth copper case in the vault beneath Borough Hall at 2:41 p.m. yesterday, to be opened in 1978. The case holds 31 records, Mr. Cyril Abbot states, among them the Armistice silence of 1928, the inauguration of March 4, and the St. Patrick's parades of 1928 and 1929. Record No. 23 is not among them. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve attended and did not speak. The vault's own house system recorded the sealing, a record 'which will be kept with the vault.'

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve's members to seal a second capsule at Flushing in June
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve stated after the sealing yesterday that the thirteen members who withdrew on Friday will seal 'a second capsule' at the Flushing Free Library in June, 'containing what the first would not.' They have asked Mr. Abbot for record No. 23.

columns.headline: Queens returns at 21,600 with one day left; Jamaica office open to midnight
columns.body: The State Tax Commission's office at Jamaica had received 21,600 Queens income tax returns for 1928 by 9 p.m. yesterday, of about 28,000 expected, and will be open until midnight tomorrow. Returns may be mailed if postmarked before midnight. The office is closed today.

columns.headline: Little America heard Saturday; the camp asks for the baseball scores
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore heard Little America at 10:22 p.m. yesterday, the camp reporting 'all well, 55 below' and asking for 'the American League schedule and any scores.' The station sent the Yankees' numbers. The camp acknowledged 'with thanks.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirteen couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m., the marathon's 174th hour.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 61. Sunday. Duke went to a meeting. Duke goes everywhere now.

lead.headline: Duke barks up the Dolan tree, and the primary gets its first watchdog
lead.deck: The Alderman's terrier turns up at the Elmhurst club uninvited; Mr. Dolan says he will not debate a dog; the dog says nothing, and says it facing Astoria
lead.body: On Friday night Mr. Dolan was explaining to the Elmhurst Democratic Club what lies under Queens when Duke of 31st Street walked in by himself, sat down at the front, and listened. Mr. Dolan said he would not debate a dog. Duke did not ask him to. At the end Duke got up, turned round, lay down facing Astoria, and was collected by the Alderman's nephew at ten. Mr. Dolan says it was a stunt. The Alderman says Duke goes where he likes. This is true; we have the clippings.

columns.headline: The fifth case goes into the vault, and No. 23 misses the cut
columns.body: Thirty-one records went into the copper case under Borough Hall yesterday, from the Armistice silence to this year's pipes, and the vault recorded itself being shut. Record No. 23 did not go in. Mrs. Grieve stood at the back and said nothing, on purpose.

columns.headline: Byrd's camp asks for the scores, and Bay Shore sends the numbers
columns.body: Little America came through last night at fifty-five below asking for the American League schedule and any scores. Bay Shore, having no scores, sent the Yankees' new numbers. The camp said thank you. Somebody down there is, we understand, a number three man.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Forest Hills throws a tax party, and it's taxing
columns.body: Darlings, a Forest Hills hostess gave a little supper last night at which every guest brought his return, and the gentlemen filled them in together over the fish while the ladies read the figures aloud. The house system has the lot. Three husbands have asked for it to be wiped.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirteen couples left at the Arena. Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant are one of them. Mr. Gant is humming slower.

record.ear: Rain. High 57. Low 46. Income tax returns due at midnight.

lead.headline: State income tax returns due at midnight; Jamaica office expects 6,000 today
lead.deck: 21,600 Queens returns received by Saturday; clerks to take returns at the counter until midnight; the office's own record to fix the time of each filing
lead.body: State income tax returns for 1928 are due at midnight tonight. The State Tax Commission's Queens office at Jamaica, which had received 21,600 returns by Saturday, expects about 6,000 today and will take them at the counter until midnight, the office's house system fixing the time of each filing 'to the second,' Deputy Commissioner Hugh Corless states. A return handed in at one second past midnight 'will be heard to be late.' Returns postmarked before midnight will be accepted.

columns.headline: Yankees beat Brooklyn 6 to 4 at Ebbets Field; Brooklyn wins Sunday 3 to 2
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Brooklyn club 6 to 4 at Ebbets Field on Saturday before about 18,000, the players wearing their numbers in New York for the first time, and Brooklyn won 3 to 2 yesterday. The Yankees open the season at the Stadium tomorrow against Boston.

columns.headline: No decision on the Riverhead seal today, the Appellate clerk states
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record will be handed down today. Mr. Gorman will attend the court at 10 a.m. 'in case.'

columns.headline: Eleven couples remain at the 198th hour of the Jamaica marathon
columns.body: Eleven couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 198th hour, the management states. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant continue. The Arena's record of the contest now runs to 412 sides and is 'stacked in the box office.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on April 10, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 57. Tax day. Pay up, Queens. The tax man is listening.

lead.headline: Tax day goes down to the wire, and Jamaica's clock has the last word
lead.deck: Six thousand stragglers due at the counter by midnight; the office's own record times each one to the second; one second late and you are heard to be late
lead.body: Tonight at midnight Queens must give the State its share of 1928, and six thousand Queens taxpayers, who have known about it since January, will be at the Jamaica office's counter between supper and the stroke. The office's house system times each return to the second. Deputy Commissioner Corless says a man who hands his in at one second past midnight will be heard to be late. The clerks say the office clock runs two minutes fast. The Commissioner says the clerks run two minutes slow.

columns.headline: Yankees wear their numbers to Flatbush, and the crowd reads them off
columns.body: The Yankees beat Brooklyn six to four at Ebbets Field on Saturday in their numbers, the first time New York has seen them, and eighteen thousand Brooklynites read the Babe's three aloud. Brooklyn won yesterday three to two. The season opens tomorrow. Bring your own arithmetic.

columns.headline: Gorman keeps his appointment, and the bench keeps him on hold
columns.body: Mr. Gorman was told April fifteenth, so he was at the Appellate Division at ten this morning, in a clean collar. The court did not decide. The clerk said so at ten past. Mr. Gorman says he can wait. He has had practice, eleven seconds' worth.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Five nights quiet, and the launches start counting fish
columns.body: WORS has not been heard since Wednesday at sixteen past eleven, when it stopped in the middle of a figure. Mr. Pike's three launches sit out every night. The North Beach crew caught forty flounder this week. The figure, wherever it is, is still unfinished.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eleven couples left at the Arena. Mrs. Corrigan has asked the band for something slow. The band has nothing faster left.
